analytic.title: Ethnicity, Gender, and the Making of a Transnational Decadent Canon: Georges Hérelle's Translations of Matilde Serao and Grazia Deledda

div.p: Traditional genealogies of decadence have placed France at the center of the movement, underlining the inspirational role of French literature and culture for writers positioned at the European periphery. Indeed, at the end of the nineteenth century, many Italian authors, writing in the context of a young nation, looked up to the works of French artists as examples of the cutting edge. This article explores the processes by which several Italian writers from this period created original work by appropriating French models, which was then exported back to France in translation. In particular, I consider the role of the French translator Georges Hérelle in the circulation of Italian works associated with decadence across languages and borders, exploring his intervention as cultural agent and gatekeeper.

Known to fin de siècle scholars as the translator of Gabriele D'Annunzio, the most internationally famous (or infamous) Italian decadent writer, Hérelle also translated other Italians whose work engages with decadent themes and style, such as Antonio Fogazzaro, Neera (Anna Zuccari), Matilde Serao, and Grazia Deledda. In this article I focus on Hérelle's relationship with Serao and Deledda, 1 two women writers from southern Italy whose works rarely feature in decadent historiographies, which are mostly dominated by male writers (their names are not mentioned, for instance, in Mario Praz's classic study The Romantic Agony [1930]). 2 This may be, in part, because of the complex or ambivalent nature of their writings. While scholars have acknowledged decadent and symbolist traits in their work, and recognized its cosmopolitan qualities, in Italy as well as abroad,

there is a tendency to align them with verismo, the Italian version of naturalism that foregrounded regional ways of life; works that depart from this strand have been generally considered less valuable. 3 In this article, I discuss the key role that Serao's and Deledda's relationships with Hérelle played in shaping international understandings of their literary affiliations. A focus on translation reveals how Hérelle and other male French intellectuals encouraged Italian female writers to minimize their cosmopolitan ambitions and stick to local inspiration in their work. As I show, Hérelle felt entitled to select and adapt Serao's and Deledda's work for a French readership, promoting features that reinforced their association with territories (Naples and Sardinia) that French readers perceived as exotic and "savage," rather than coeval with modern Western societies. He also relentlessly discouraged Deledda and Serao from experimenting with foreign languages and assimilating European (and especially French) literary influences. In doing so, he and his collaborators effectively treated them, to use Gayatri Spivak's terminology, as "native informants," whose task was to recount and interpret their native traditions for the enjoyment and consumption of nonnative readerships. 4 In this article, I draw on Hérelle's correspondence and on his memoirs in order to uncover the different strategies he used with male and female writers, and the effect that his actions as a translator-editor had on these writers' international reception. Examining what drew Hérelle to Serao and Deledda, and which changes their work underwent as it was received in a French context, reveal some of the ways that women's participation in transnational literary neworks was mediated, regulated, and in some cases limited by male agents. Hérelle's interventions had long-term repercussions in shaping transnational canons of decadence. His actions influenced the international circulation of Serao's and Deledda's work in translation and affected their ambitions and their literary production. In what follows, I first outline Hérelle's links to Italian decadence through his relationship with D'Annunzio, and then consider in turn his treatment of Serao and Deledda. Hérelle's approach to his role as a translator provides important evidence about the role played by the intersection of ethnicity 3. On the fluctuation of these writers between verismo and decadentismo, and the tendency to associate them with the former, see the editors' introduction to Matilde Serao: International Profile, Reception and Networks, ed. 4. Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, A Critique of Postcolonial Reason: Toward a History of the Vanishing Present (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1999), 6. Elisa Segnini • Ethnicity, Gender, and a Decadent Canon and gender within the French reception of Italian decadentismo, and within the international circulation of decadence more broadly.
GEORGES H ÉRELL E: A " DECADENT" T RA N S L A TO R U NA W A R E OF DECADENCE?

Hérelle's activity as a translator has been well documented by French and Italian scholars, including Guy Tosi, Marie Martin-Gistucci, Maddalena Rasera, and Guy Ducrey. 5 For my purposes, I would like to draw attention to three characteristic elements of his approach: first, his friendship with intellectuals closely affiliated with decadence; second, his conservative stance regarding the purpose and function of translation; and third, the curious tension that emerges between his own aesthetic values and those of the works he translated. These factors are vital to understanding his relationships with Serao and Deledda.

Hérelle's work on D'Annunzio was closely associated with his friendship with the critic and novelist Paul Bourget. According to the Italian critic and translator Enrico Nencioni, Bourget embodied the psychic and intellectual state of a generation unable to come to terms with the scientific principles of positivism. 6 His writing, Nencioni noted in 1909, prefigured decadent aesthetics by going beyond realist conventions and contributing to an atmosphere "di dubbio, di indecisione, di debolezza della volontà, di malaise, di tormento" (of doubt, indecision, impasse of the will, malaise, anguish). 7 As a critic, Bourget aided the identification of decadent themes and provided a definition of decadent style that became widely knownnamely, as writing that draws attention to individual words and sentences at the expense of the whole. 8 It was to Bourget that Hérelle reached out in 1892 to publish the French translation of D'Annunzio's L'innocente (The innocent) (1892). 9 The fact that Hérelle used Bourget as an intermediary to promote D'Annunzio's fame internationally shows that he was aware of the fine tuning between the two writers and recognized similarities between their works. After the publication of Hérelle's French translation of Il piacere (Pleasure) (1889) in 1895, D'Annunzio would in fact be accused of drawing too conspicuously from Bourget's texts. From his end, Bourget praised Hérelle's French translation of Trionfo della morte (Triumph of death) (1894) as a masterpiece, and commented that the Italian writer was lucky to have as a translator "un des meilleurs écrivains de ce temps-ci, auquel j'ai toujours dit qu'il ne lui manquait qu'un peu de confiance et d'ambition" (one of the best writers of our time, to whom I have always said that he only lacked a little confidence and ambition). 10 Through his work on D'Annunzio and then Fogazzaro, Hérelle became familiar with the musical prose and complex language used by Italian decadents, as well as with their favorite settings (e.g., a decaying, aristocratic world) and with themes prominent in Italian decadent literature (a heightened nervous sensibility, indulgence in pleasure, exoticism, and the mixing of religion and sensuality). Further, the reception of his translation of Il piacere exposed Hérelle to critical discourses around decadence and aestheticism: D'Annunzio's novel was compared to Huysmans's À rebours (1884), and its protagonist was described as an "esthète, au sens anglais du mot" (aesthete, in the English sense of the word), inspired by Burne-Jones, Ruskin, and Tennyson. 11 Although Hérelle made a name for himself as a mediator for Italian decadence in France, his relationship with decadence was, in fact, more complex than any simple or direct affiliation. As Guy Ducrey notes, in his person Hérelle might be thought to embody the spirit of decadence on several grounds: he posed as an amateur and a collector and led a private life as a homosexual man that was at odds with contemporary mores. 12 His public position, however, was that of a lycée professor and scrupulous scholar of the local history of the Champagne and Basque regions of France. At the same time, his respectable scholarly activities intersected with his transgressive interests; the personal historical archives that Hérelle amassed also included extensive material on the history of homosexuality. Toward the end of his life, he donated all these papers to the library of Troyes. He also transcribed some of the letters exchanged with the editors of the journals in which his translations were published, while others are preserved in the Bibliothèque nationale de France. Today, most of this material has been published, although it is not yet available in English translation. 12. Ducrey, "Is There Such a Thing," 18.

Elisa Segnini • Ethnicity, Gender, and a Decadent Canon Indeed, Hérelle's role as a translator of D'Annunzio's decadent writings is cognate with these tensions and apparent contradictions between his personal and private life. As part of his archival work, there is a manuscript that remained unpublished during his lifetime, entitled "Petits mémoires littéraires," where Hérelle introduces his literary, philosophical, and anthropological works for posterity. As Clive Thomson has noted, these "Petits mémoires" are extremely restrained about Hérelle's inquiries into homosexuality, which were either not printed or were issued under pseudonym. 13 I would suggest that a similar attitude characterizes his attraction for Italian decadentismo: it was both something that he felt heavily drawn to and, at the same time, something that needed to be domesticated and controlled so that it did not interfere with his public image.

In an 1898 interview with Il Marzocco, a journal closely associated with D'Annunzio, Hérelle defined his interest in Italian literature as that of an "amateur." Commenting on the place of Italian literature among the literatures of modern Europe, he noted that Giovanni Pascoli-the foremost Italian poet associated with decadence-remained unknown in France, and that Fogazzaro's and Serao's reception was still limited. Only Gabriele D'Annunzio, he wrote (implicitly underlining his own role as a gatekeeper), had gathered admiration by producing "oeuvres empreintes d'une originalité profonde et resplendissantes d'une étrange beauté" (works imprinted with profound originality and resplendent with a strange beauty). 14 Similarly, Hérelle declared in his memoirs that he read very little and never followed contemporary critical debates, whether in France or abroad. 15 When he mentioned symbolism, it was to make the point that it is always reductive to force artists into individual categories. 16 For Hérelle, D'Annunzio was not the bard of the French-inspired decadentismo, but an Italian writer free of foreign influence who had been able to revive Italian literature after a period of decadence. 17 Strategically, this insistence upon D'Annunzio's originality served to defend the Italian author from accusations of imitation and plagiarism, but it also also distanced him from international literary trends.

His interview provides confirmation for Ducrey's claim that Hérelle's translation of D'Annunzio sought to diminish the symbolist and decadent aesthetics of his works-a concern that was also voiced by critics during Hérelle's time. 18 For in his role as a mediator between D'Annunzio and editors of prestigious French journals, Hérelle encouraged cuts that reduced the sexual imagery and the antidemocratic spirit of his novels. Where Bourget, following Désiré Nisard and Théophile Gautier, had argued that decadence was characterized by variegated language and a self-conscious style, Hérelle made linguistic choices that tended to neutralize the decadent quality of D'Annunzio's precious, obscure prose, rendering it in elegant but nevertheless standard academic French. 19 D'Annunzio himself was first to recognize this, complaining that Hérelle's "clear and fluid" language erased the tormented research of his prose, and demanding that his writing be rendered in all its stylistic complexity, including flaws. 20 As Hérelle recalled it, their disagreements reached a peak during his translation of the musical prose of Il fuoco (The flame) (1900), when D'Annunzio returned his French translation with "mauvaises corrections" (bad corrections) filled with "solecismes et barbarismes" (distorted syntax and foreign words). 21 Drawing on the correspondence between Hérelle and D'Annunzio, and on Hérelle's sharp criticism of experimental decadent translations, Ducrey concludes that Hérelle was unable to detect the innovations of urban movements such as symbolism and decadence due to his provincial background. 22 The use of the terms "solecismes" and "barbarismes," however, suggests that Hérelle was more familiar with the discourse of decadence than he was willing to acknowledge, for these are the same features (and the same words) that Charles Baudelaire used to describe the characteristic traits of the decadent language of exhausted civilizations in a note to "Franciscae meae laudes," his Latin poem within the first edition of Les fleurs du mal (1857). 23 Curiously, Hérelle did not take issue with solecisms and barbarisms in D'Annunzio's Italian, which is filled with archaisms, neologisms, and foreign terms. He could not, however, conceive of transposing such idiosyncrasies into French.

As Blaise Wilfert-Portal has argued, linguistic inventiveness and plurilingualism were crucial ingredients of a subversive aesthetic for French symbolist and decadent writers. By the time Hérelle began his career as a translator, this experimental phase had ended, and foreign influences had become associated with threats to the purity of French language and literature. In this setting, translation continued to be practiced but assumed the conservative function of enabling French intellectuals to construct ideas and canons of foreign literatures. 24 In this light, Hérelle's commitment to defending the "Frenchness" of the language used by prestigious journals in works of translation foregrounds his conservative stance. 25 I suggest that Hérelle's disavowal of decadence comes close to the Freudian concept of Verleugnung (denial), a mechanism through which a subject rejects something obvious but too uncomfortable to process. This blind spot concerning decadence enabled him to engage with writers associated with Italian decadentismo and yet to present them as "original" and "different" from French decadents, effacing aspects of their work inspired by French sources. He thus satisfied his unspoken attraction for decadence, while at the same time presenting these works in a fluid French prose that did not threaten French linguistic norms and, by extension, reactionary contemporary mores. Hérelle recalls how he took to reading the Corriere di Napoli during his second trip to Naples in 1891 because Serao's chronicles amused him. Back in Cherbourg, he subscribed to the newspaper, and it was here (in Hérelle's account) that he came across D'Annunzio's L'innocente, was "ébloui" (dazzled) by it, and began translating it out of pleasure. 26 Thus Serao featured from the outset as a mediator between D'Annunzio and Hérelle. She had publicly defended L'innocente, and D'Annunzio dedicated Giovanni Episcopo to her in 1891. In 1893, when Hérelle intended to write an article on Serao, D'Annunzio gave him permission on her behalf to cite from Il paese della cuccagna (The land of Cockaigne) (1890), the book Serao considered her masterpiece. Upon his return from a cruise on the Aegan sea with D'Annunzio and Scarfoglio in 1895, Hérelle spent time in Naples and was often invited for lunch by Serao, who asked him to translate some of her works. So it is most likely jealousy that prompted D'Annunzio to affirm that he was unfamiliar with Serao's books in a letter to Hérelle from 1896. Nevertheless, he pointed the translator in the direction of the collection Il romanzo della fanciulla (Novel by a young woman) (1886), which included the story "Telegrafi dello stato" (State telegraphs) (1884). 27 In turn, Serao was influenced to some extent by D'Annunzio and, like him, found her models in French literature. However, she was more committed to realism. Stylistically, her fiction is hard to place: as Tommaso Scappaticci notes, she came close to verismo when portraying working-class Naples, but adopted decadent tones and themes when describing the life of the upper classes. 28 Unlike D'Annunzio, who took an antidemocratic stance, she displayed an interest for the life of the poor. Her early writings in particular address political and social issues, although admittedly her activism was limited: her stories are far from undermining the established order and calling for interclass reconciliation. The novels set among the aristocracy are filled with femmes fatales and dandies, sexual fantasies, eroticism, and intense emotions.

The use of a register close to spoken language, with structures and words adapted from Neapolitan, combined with the frequent use of neologisms, sophisticated terms, and French influences, earned Serao a reputation for "writing badly." Before marrying her, Scarfoglio had criticized her hybrid language and accused her of borrowing too much from French authors. He described her prose as "una minestra fatta di tutti gli avanzi di un banchetto copioso, nella quale certi stracci stranamente tinti nuotano in una broda incolore, nella quale certi pimenti troppo forti tentano invano di saporire la scipitaggine dell'insieme. La sua lingua poverissima vi si dissolve sotto le mani per la inesattezza, per la inopportunità, per la miscela dei vocaboli dialettali italiani e francesi" (a soup made up of all the leftovers of a copious banquet, in which some strangely dyed rags swim in a colorless soup, in which certain spices that are too strong try in vain to savor the insipid whole. Her very poor language dissolves under our hands due to the inaccuracy, the inopportunity, the mixture of dialect words, Italian and French). 29 While such prose differed from the sophisticated style of D'Annunzio, it was driven by the same urgent desire to renew the Italian language by drawing both on foreign sources (with the overwhelming influence of French) and domestic resources (Latin and Greek etymology for D'Annunzio, Neapolitan for Serao). It is in this respect that Serao's prose came close to the linguistic experiments of the decadents and symbolists.

Antonia Arslan describes Serao as a "grande cosmopolita" (great cosmopolitan) close to international intellectuals and up to date with the latest innovations and trends in the Anglophone and Francophone world of the time. 30 Accordingly, by the time Hérelle expressed interest in translating her work, Serao had already asked her friends Count Primoli and Paul Bourget to mediate for her with French publishers. In her first letter to Hérelle, Serao expressed her delight at the prospect of being translated by "le meilleur, le plus haut collaborateur de Gabriele d'Annunzio" (the best, the highest collaborator of Gabriele d'Annunzio), to whom she attributed "la moitié et bien plus, de ses success [sic] en France" (half and much more of his successes in France). She regretted that Il paese della cuccagna had already been promised to Minnie Bourget, the wife of Paul Bourget, and asked Hérelle to forgive her for her "francese di fantasia" (invented French). 31 Among the writers translated by Hérelle, Serao is, interestingly, the only one who consistently wrote to him in French. This demonstrates her profound cosmopolitanism but also her confidence in her status as a well-known, internationally respected public figure whose works were read across Europe. It also implies an ensuing belief that her correspondent will therefore not judge her for her mistakes, which include misplaced accents, altered words, and awkward grammar. This trust, as we shall see, was misplaced, for despite Serao's international reputation, Hérelle did not hesitate to undermine her with French colleagues.

div.head: M O D E R N P H I L O L O G Y
div.p: Following D'Annunzio's assessment, Hérelle translated "Telegrafi dello stato," together with "All'erta, sentinella!" (Alert, sentry!) (1888) and "Terno secco" (Three winning numbers) (1888), which were published in the Revue de Paris and then issued as a volume by Calmann-Lévy in 1899 (the same publisher used by D'Annunzio). These stories, which feature a multiplicity of characters, offering sketches of historical Naples and local mores, were a decade old by the time Hérelle published them. Following their success in the Revue de Paris, Hérelle translated Giovannino o la morte (Giovannino or death) (1888), a novella in which Serao had adopted local words and syntax to offer a glimpse of life in a Neapolitan palazzo, featuring a sentimental romance that resolved with the protagonist's suicide. Aware that the setting constituted one of the strength of the piece, he added a footnote to the term palais to indicate that "en Italie, et surtout à Naples, on donne le nom de palazzi à de grandes maisons particulières que nous appellerions 'hotels,' et souvent même à de simples maisons de rapport" (in Italy, and especially in Naples, the name palazzi is given to large private houses that we would call "hotels," and often even to simple multifamily houses). 32 In this note, his tone is that of an ethnographer respectful of local language use. It is clear that he saw mediation with the target audience as his own responsibility. However, he made no effort to render the idiosyncrasies of Serao's style: for instance, he translated a Neapolitan song into standard French, with no footnotes indicating that it was in dialect in the original. While Hérelle's choice of Neapolitan pieces reflects an almost anthropological interest in the city, his translation strategies thus relied on domestication. By using standard French, he obliterated Serao's multilingualism and the contrast between the regional and the national. This did not seem to matter much to Serao, who after reading Ou Giovannino ou la mort! in the Revue de Paris confessed to Hérelle that she enjoyed the story in translation more than the original: "Comme vous interpretez les intentions d'un ecrivain! Vous etes un magicien, vraiment" (How well you interpret the intentions of a writer! You are a magician, really). 33 By this time, Serao had achieved considerable popularity in France, and her writing had become known through translations by women writers, including Minnie Bourget, Jean D'Arcy, Charles Laurent, and Nelly Carrère. But none of these women had Hérelle's reputation or status. Serao identified Hérelle with the success of D'Annunzio in France and was thus keen to continue working with him. In 1899, she visited Paris and had breakfast with Louis Ganderax, the director of the Revue de Paris, promising him "un 32. Translator's note in Matilde Serao, Ou Giovannino ou la mort! (Paris: Calmann-Lévy, 1900), 5.
33. Serao to Hérelle, May 15, 1899, in Giglio, Per la storia, 159. All quotations from Serao retain any errors in French grammar, spelling, and accents in the original.

Elisa Segnini • Ethnicity, Gender, and a Decadent Canon grand roman de moeurs napolitaines" (a great novel of Neapolitan customs). 34 But she had nothing available and no time to write something new, so she suggested that Hérelle choose a story from Le amanti (The lovers) (1894), since she had just recovered authorial rights to that volume. Unlike her work published in the 1880s, these tales are psychological studies of erotism among the aristocracy. Hérelle's choice fell on "Tramontando il sole" (As the sun sets), a tale of passion against the background of a picturesque Neapolitan landscape, which Tommaso Scappaticci describes as "a decadent version" of Verga's La lupa (The she-wolf) 35 -in other words, a story that echoed Verga's iconic story, but through a decadent lens.

Meanwhile, in 1897, Serao had met Ferdinand Brunetière, director of the prestigious Revue des Deux Mondes, in which D'Annunzio's writings were regularly published, and she had arranged to write for him a new piece, also referred to as "un roman napolitaine" (a Neapolitan novel). 36 While the Revue de Paris had so far published mostly older pieces, La ballerina (The dancer) was the first short novel written from the outset for a French readership. Like her pieces of the 1880s, it was set in working-class Naples and focused on Carmela Minino, a poor dancer of the San Carlo Theatre secretly in love with an aristocrat. Unlike Serao's early pieces, however, it featured an atmosphere of introspection and pity that resonated with Bourget's concerns in Essays de psychologie contemporaine (1883) and with the emphasis placed by the French critic Melchior de Vogüé on mysticism and on "la religion de la souffrance" (the religion of suffering) in the influential volume Le roman russe (The Russian novel) (1886). 37 Serao's article "I cavalieri del santo spirito" (Knights of the Holy Spirit), published on July 8, 1894, in Il mattino di Napoli, demonstrates that she was familiar with these publications. That article credits the much-admired Fogazzaro and her friend Bourget among writers associated with a new form of religiosity that enabled the overcoming of realism. She also knew that Brunetière, who was very religious and had recently converted to Catholicism, sympathized with these trends. With La ballerina, Serao was obviously trying to please Brunetière by providing a folkloristic view of Naples that she knew would appeal to French readerships in search of exoticism, while at the same time engaging with transnational trends. Religion had always been an important theme for Serao, a committed Catholic whose fiction often mixed erotism and Catholicism. The embrace of mysticism in La ballerina, however, went beyond this, and signaled her effort to follow in the footsteps of D'Annunzio and Fogazzaro who, by mixing Italian subject matters and French-influenced style, had been successful in placing their works in a transnational canon of decadence.

As we learn from a letter to Brunetière, Hérelle did not appreciate Serao's new story and undermined her work with the French critic. This Italian woman, he noted, was trying too hard to second-guess the taste of French readers, and thus produced a "very Neapolitan" novel, but the effort to imitate French models led to some confusion: "Pour faire très napolitain, elle a multiplié les détails descriptifs, et elle s'y est un peu perdue; pour faire très 'Revue des Deux Mondes' elle a mêlé à son napolitanisme des pages d'art et d'éloquence" (To sound very Neapolitan, she has multiplied descriptive details, and she got a little lost in them; to make it very "Revue des Deux Mondes," she has mixed pages of art and eloquence with her Neapolitanism). In the same letter, Hérelle notified Brunetière that he had improved her text by correcting historical references and factual details and by cutting repetitions: "Quel intérêt y a-t-il à répéter une demi-douzaine de fois que les chaussons de danse coutent pour le moins 4 francs? Que, dans la chambrée des figurantes, la chaleur, les sueurs, les haleines et les parfums à bon marché forment une atmosphère qui sent très mauvais? . . . De telles particularités ne sont ni napolitaines, ni parisiennes: elles sont universelles" (What's the point of repeating half a dozen times that ballet slippers cost at least 4 francs? That, in the room of the extras, heat, sweats, breaths, and cheap perfumes form an atmosphere that smells very bad? . . . Such distinctive features are neither Neapolitan nor Parisian: they are universal). 38 Hérelle could only appreciate realism, we infer from this comment, insofar as it contributed to local color. In Serao's story, however, such details did not conjure picturesque views of Naples, and he thus interpreted them as vulgar, as a symptom of bad taste, too close to the naturalism of Zola. Eager to publish in the Revue des Deux Mondes, Serao approved unconditionally all corrections, even commenting that La ballerina would surely gain in translation. 39 Suor Giovanna della Croce (Sister Giovanna of the Cross) (1891), a second novella written for the Revue des Deux Mondes, further emphasized the focus on suffering and decadent religiosity that Serao knew to be popular with French intellectuals. The prefatory dedication to Bourget, whom she addressed as "friend and teacher," made Serao's attempt to insert herself into a transnational canon of avant-garde mystical writers even clearer. 40 In this story, a nun is forced to leave her convent after the abolition of her religious 38. Hérelle to Brunetière, May 24, 1899, in Martin-Gistucci, "Matilde Serao et Ferdinand Brunetière," 106-7.
39. Serao to Hérelle, June 8, 1899, in Giglio, Per la storia, 160. 40. Matilde Serao, "A Paolo Bourget," Suor Giovanna della croce (Milan, 1891), xiii.

Elisa Segnini • Ethnicity, Gender, and a Decadent Canon order. Unable to adapt to the world after many years in a secluded environment, she is first exploited by her relatives, then forced out and exposed to moral degradation. The conjunction of a Neapolitan environment with these religious themes resonated with Brunetière, but was not appreciated by Hérelle, who liked strong, Mediterranean passions. In his introduction to D'Annunzio's Episcopo et Cie, published in 1895, Hérelle had praised D'Annunzio's subtle analysis of crimes, moral anomalies, madness, and idolatry. 41 It is not surprising that he found Suor Giovanna della Croce boring. Writing to Brunetiére, he noted that Serao's intention to portray humble, selfeffacing subjects came too close to banality: "Que Soeur Jeanne marmotte des prières en relavant la vaisselle, c'est fort bien; mais il me plairait qu'au milieu de ces vulgaires occupations elle donnait quelques signes d'une pensée forte et d'une grande âme" (It's fine that Soeur Jeanne mumbles prayers while washing the dishes; but I would like it if, in the midst of these vulgar occupations, she gave some signs of a strong mind and a great soul.) 42 The story was published in the Neapolitan magazine Flegrea, then in Il mattino, and sent to Hérelle immediately afterward. But Hérelle was busy translating D'Annunzio's Il fuoco in January 1900, and his work on Serao proceeded at a slow pace. When she received the proofs, Serao was horrified by his "atrocious" cuts and, for the first time, defended her style: "Chaque phrase, chaque mot, je l'ai employé avec une ideé! Il y a même de répétitions voulues, de mots qui ont une valeur spéciale!" (Each sentence, each word, I used it with an idea! There are even intentional repetitions, words that have a special value!) 43 These were the same words that D'Annunzio, in his exchange with the Italian publisher Treves, has used to defend repetitions in L'innocente, which in his view were essential for the musical quality of the work and inspired by "deep artistic reasons." 44 Although she finally consented to cuts in the journal publication, it was on condition that the original version be restated in the volume. Three months later, she conceded in a letter that she had accepted Hérelle's corrections previously, but that she had done so only because they concerned older works. The case of Soeur Jeanne de la Croix, she argued, was different, because this was a work written "mot à mot" (word by word). Proffering a very similar argument to D'Annunzio, who insisted Hérelle make an effort to preserve his style, she asked Hérelle for a "traduction un peu littérale" (a translation that is a little literal). Her thoughts on translation had changed. Now that she professed a poetics that resonated with symbolist and decadent credos, she insisted on a word-by-word approach at the expense of the fluidity of the whole text, privileging, as Bourget put it, the part at the expense of the whole.

In an undated letter of the same year, she went further and, using almost the same words as D'Annunzio, demanded that her style be rendered in all its flaws and idiosyncrasies: "Il m'est impossible d'ouvrir avec mes critiques et avec vous une polémique sur mes défauts littéraires; c'est à dire le désordre, la confusion, la rípetition. Je prefère les accepter comme un fait: j'ai donc cés défauts, mais dans ma nouvelle Soeur Jeanne de la croix je tiens à mes défauts, du commencement jusqu'à la fin. Je vous prie, donc, même en faisant un sacrifice, de voulouir faire les reconstitution et les corrections que je vous ai demandeès, toutes" (It is impossible for me to open a polemic on my literary faults with my critics and with you; that is, disorder, confusion, repetition. I prefer to accept them as a fact: so I have these faults, but in the novella Soeur Jeanne de la croix I care about these faults, from beginning to end. I beg you, therefore, even if this involves a sacrifice, to carry through all the reconstructions and the corrections that I have asked you to make, all of them). 45 For the volume edited by Calmann Lévy, Serao planned, following influential French models (Balzac, and especially Zola), to present La danseuse (the dancer) and Soeur Jeanne de la Croix as the first novels of a cycle titled "l'âme simple" (the simple soul). Hérelle and Calmann Lévy, however, took out all references to a cycle because they wanted Serao's works to sound original and different, rather than akin to French models. They also changed the title of Soeur Jeanne de la Croix to Vie en détresse (Life in distress), thus emphasizing the connection to the themes of verismo (poverty, exasperation, etc.) and lessening the focus on religiosity. 46 The volume marked the end of Serao's collaboration with the Revue des Deux Mondes. Hérelle continued to translate Serao's works for the Revue de Paris, but with diminishing enthusiasm. 47 If the history of Serao's writing for the Revue des Deux Mondes shows Hérelle's disapproval toward her adoption of mysticism and symbolist or decadent themes, his dealings with the last novels she published in the Revue de Paris demonstrate his resistance to the Italian writer's distancing herself from her ethnic background. Hérelle Elisa Segnini • Ethnicity, Gender, and a Decadent Canon of dramatic alpine landscapes. In a letter to Hérelle, Serao thanked him for the translation, which she described as "magnifique." 48 To her friend Count Primoli, however, she complained of the translation's poor quality, noting that when Hérelle did not like a novel, he translated it terribly. 49 As Vive la vie! was about to be published in volume form, Serao stressed that the multilingual fabric of the novel was an essential part of its cosmopolitanism, and instructed Hérelle to restore those sentences in foreign languages that had been translated into French for the publication in the Revue de Paris. 50 D'Annunzio had made a similar request for the translation of Il piacere, which, like Evviva la vita!, featured an aristocratic environment and multilingual characters. Hérelle, who stood firm on the ground that "une traduction française doit être écrite en français" (a French translation must be written in French), only partially and grudgingly complied with Serao's request. 51 He reinserted some, but not all of the English words, adding footnotes with French translations even for intuitive terms like "mum" or "deary." 52 While he kept most of the French expressions used by Serao, he did not use italics or footnotes to signal that they featured in French in the original. As for German words and sentences, he translated them all into French, except for characters' names or topographical references. In light of the proximity of war, the strategy was undoubtedly a political one. The homogenizing effect of his translation is evident at first glance: whereas Serao's original Italian text is continually disrupted by words in italics, in Hérelle's French version the few foreign words merge with the rest of the narrative, flattening the cosmopolitan effect that Serao sought. Even though his prestige contributed to the transnational dissemination of Serao, Hérelle saw limits in what this Neapolitan woman could competently write about, did not appreciate her assimilation of French and Russian sources, and sought to narrow her work in scope.

div.head: TH E " P E T I T E S A R D E" AND T HE EMINENT TRANSLATOR
div.p: On May 6, 1903, Serao complimented Hérelle on his translation of Grazia Deledda's Elias Portolu (1900), but noted that the subject was "trop special à la Sardaigne" (too specific to Sardinia). 53 The period during which Hérelle translated Deledda was characterized by a break from his translation of D'Annunzio and his investigations of homosexuality, during which he dedicated himself to the study of Basque theater. 54 In his memoirs, Hérelle recalls how Brunetière asked him in 1901 whether Deledda's Elias Portolu would be worth publishing in the Revue des Deux Mondes. Hérelle made clear that the book was not a masterpiece and could not be compared to L'innocente. Nevertheless, he argued that it had all the features that make a foreign novel worth translating: "Il était simple de sujet et de forme, il m'initiait aux moeurs d'un pays resté primitive et un peu barbare, il ne ressemblait à aucune livre français connu de moi" (It was simple in subject and form, it introduced me to the mores of a country that had remained primitive and a little barbaric, it did not resemble any French book I knew). 55 The only inconvenience, he remarked, was that it resembled Verga's I Malavoglia (1881), but Hérelle noted that Deledda's book had the advantage of displaying "moins des 54. It is also significant that Hérelle came to Elias Portolu having translated La barraca by the Spanish writer Blasco Ibañez, whose work held a similar appeal for its descriptions of local mores.
55. Hérelle, Petit mémoire, 32.

Elisa Segnini • Ethnicity, Gender, and a Decadent Canon grossièretés" (fewer vulgarities) than Verga's. 56 Hérelle voices here a preoccupation with originality that he never expressed in relation to D'Annunzio's work. In the process, he also reveals a puritan vein that underlines the distance between his private and public persona. Recognizing Elias Portolu as a "moral" example of verismo, Hérelle appreciated Deledda's novel because it was deeply rooted in Sardinian culture, finding in it the taste for the archaic that had drawn him to Basque theater, and the visceral passions that had fascinated him in L'innocente. For the French translator, as he underlines in the preface to Elias Portolu, Sardinia was a mysterious land, a remote island that remained outside the narrative of modernity and that preserved "coutumes qui remontent aux temps homériques" (customs that date back to Homeric times). 57 Deledda encouraged this interpretation. Just as D'Annunzio had sent to Hérelle a fictional biography tailored to French readers that stressed his links to Abruzzo and his exceptional upbringing, her second letter to Hérelle included a brief biography that can be defined as self-exoticizing: "Io non ho fatto mai studi, sono nata e vissuta in un piccolo paese di Sardegna, fra le montagne selvagge e solitarie sotto un cielo orientale, da un popolo e fra un popolo sul quale pare gravi una strana fatalità di tristezza" (I have never studied, I was born and lived in a small town in Sardinia, among the wild and lonely mountains under an oriental sky, from a people and among a people on whom seems to loom a strange fatality of sadness.) 58 In the same letter, while acknowledging that she could read French, she thanked Hérelle for the offer to intervene in the translations and submissively noted that she would never dare to correct him.

Deledda's texts can be seen as containing translation from the start, even before they started circulating across national borders. Her native language was the dialect of Nuoro: she had learned Italian as a foreign language and was known for writing with a dictionary. Like Serao, she was accused by contemporary critics of "writing badly," for thinking in dialect and translating into Italian. Indeed, her prose features calques from Sardinian dialect terms and expressions; she models sentence structures after Sardinian grammar. As Massimo Pittau noted, these features occur especially in indirect or direct discourse, and since they are absent when Deledda conjures landscapes or uses non-Sardinian settings, they must therefore be understood as a conscious stylistic choice. 59 Hérelle ignored all this, and, in the same letter to Brunetière containing his verdict on Elias Portolu, he confirmed that Deledda's prose was easily transferable into French. 60 His stance toward dialect, as we have seen from his translation of Serao's novel, was that it should be rendered into standard French. In Petit mémoire d'un traducteur, he even theorized this, noting that the effect conjured by the "emploi accidental" (accidental use) of dialect is untranslatable, and that it would be absurd to make a character from Vicenza speak the Norman patois or a Neapolitan the Auvergnant patois. His solution was to disregard the effect of dialect altogether and to translate such passages as if they were written in standard language. 61 This view conformed with the defense of Frenchness preached by conservatives such as Brunetière. In his memoirs, Hérelle acknowledges that he intentionally "francified" (to use D'Annunzio's term) D'Annunzio's Episcopo et Cie and all Fogazzaro's prose, rendering sentences in dialect into standard French. 62 Such comments demonstrate Hérelle's disregard of questions of regional and national identities, power, and subalternity raised by the use of dialect. He was, however, more receptive to the aesthetic function of dialect: he grants that, in some instances, sentences in nonstandard language may have "une valeur rythmique qui lui est propre" (a rhythmic value of their own). 63 As examples of such types of texts, he mentions D'Annunzio's drama La Gioconda (1899) and Deledda's novels, thus implicitly underlining the importance of musical prose in both authors. In both cases, he recalls, he reproduced the original lines in footnotes to enable French readers to access the original. By placing Deledda's lyrical use of dialect and D'Annunzio's multilingual experiments into the same category, Hérelle betrays an intuition that he is not willing to acknowledge openly-namely, that there are strong similarities between the two writers. But after making this statement, he immediately imposes a contrast between the two authors by recalling the approach taken in Elias Portolu, which seems contrary to all his rules and criteria: "Néanmoins, dans Elias Portolu, il m'est arrivé, je ne sais pas pourquoi, de mettre en note la traduction française" (Nevertheless, in Elias Portolu, it came natural to me, I do not know why, to add the French translation in footnotes). 64 Hérelle's account is a testament to his effort to present Elias Portolu as an ethnic document on the customs and mores of Sardinia, rather than as a literary text. It is also an example of how, despite his awareness of similarities between the two writers, his translation strategies deliberately established a distance between Deledda's and D'Annunzio's works.

This stance also emerges from his judgment of Deledda's short story, Un'aberrazione (An aberration) (1901). We can infer from a response by Deledda during October 1901 that Hérelle judged the story too heavily influenced by Dostoevsky and advised her not to have it translated. This is a curious verdict, since the first work by D'Annunzio that had fascinated him was L'innocente, a novel strongly influenced by Dostoevsky and celebrated in France by the slavist Melchior de Vogüé. Deledda tried to justify her story by underlining the originality of her approach-namely, the transposition of modern literary influences into a rural context. She clarified that she had heard the story from a Sardinian student who had fallen ill after reading Crime and Punishment and had the same ideas as Dostoevsky's protagonist; and she claimed that Russians and Sardinians resembled one another, as both remained "un po' barbari" (a little barbarian). However, she submissively accepted Hérelle's judgment and promised that she would send for translation only "cose mie perfettamente originali" (my indisputably original things). 65 The contrast between Hérelle's treatment of Deledda as a woman writer and her male peer D'Annunzio is striking. Hérelle had never been concerned by D'Annunzio's rewritings of foreign sources, even strenuously defending him from accusations of plagiarism. But he was deeply bothered that Deledda's inspiration should come from beyond Italy. The translator's emphasis on originality, in his correspondence with Deledda, thus served to deter the writer from engaging with contemporary, international trends.

To prove her point about similarities between the Russian and Sardinian way of life, Deledda promised to send to Hérelle La via del male (The path of evil), a novel published in 1896 and set among Sardinian peasants. The novel was originally titled L'indomabile (The indomitable), a fin de siècle title that recalled L'invincibile, D'Annunzio's original title for Trionfo della morte. Deledda's book was filled with references to the cult of the Übermensch as inspired by Nietzsche's Zarathustra (1883-85) and adapted by D'Annunzio. Hérelle asked Deledda to revise several episodes, and Deledda patiently carried out the requested modifications around 1903. As the French translation remained unpublished, however, she warned Hérelle in 1905 that she was working on a new Italian edition. Euralio De Michelis notes that the new version of La via del male, published in La Gazzetta del Popolo di Torino in 1906, got rid of the Dannunzian influences and brought the novel decisively in line with the conventions of verismo. 66 Deledda's revisions respond to the judgment of influential Italian critics, such as Luigi Capuana, who encouraged Deledda to stay focused on Sardinian mores. Maddelena Rasera has, however, demonstrated that Hérelle's feedback also had an important impact, for the corrections that Deledda implemented during 1903 in response to his criticisms were all maintained in the 1906 Italian edition. 67 Hérelle eventually translated from the 1906 manuscript, and La vie du mal appeared in the Revue de Paris from May to July 1908 before being published the following year by Calmann-Lévy. According to Rasera, this is, among Hérelle's translations of Deledda, "the most faithful to the original." 68 Indeed, having contributed to the expurgation of decadent features from the text, Hérelle himself considered the revised version of La via del male Deledda's best work.

The publication of Cenere was a different affair. Aware of Hérelle's specific interest in Sardinia, Deledda tried to downplay the Roman elements, presenting the novel as a work "di argomento sardo" (Sardinian in topic). 69 Before publication in the Revue des Deux Mondes, Brunetière drew on Hérelle's judgment, asking for several changes and requesting that she rewrite the ending. As Rasera notes, Hérelle only partially followed Deledda's corrections as he made cuts, moved scenes, and summarized evocative descriptions in a few lines. His Petit mémoire reproduces a letter by Brunetière about the translation of Cenere to demonstrate the trust the prestigious editor had in him as a translator: "Taillez et coupez à votre mesure et au gré de vos scrupules d'art, dont Mme Deledda n'aura, j'en suis sûr, que à se féliciter. Et d'ailleurs, ainsi qu'il convient, renvoyez-moi la responsabilité de toute que vous aurez dû faire. Heureux ces Italiens, de vous avoir pour collaborateur autant et plus que pour traducteur" (Trim and cut as you wish and according to your artistic scruples. Mme Deledda, I am sure, will benefit from it. And, as agreed, blame me for what you will have to do. Happy these Italians, to have you as a collaborator as well a translator). 70 This confirms what the correspondence with Serao shows-namely, that Hérelle's role went far beyond that of a translator and that he effectively acted as an editor and, I argue, coauthor of the Italian writers he translated. It also fleshes out his pride in this role.

The original letter preserved among Brunetière's papers at the Bibliothèque nationale, however, reveals that Hérelle censored a few lines of the correspondence. In this copy, the same passage reads: "Taillez et coupez à votre mesure et au gré de vos scrupules d'art, dont Mme Deledda n'aura, j'en sui sûr, que à se féliciter et, d'ailleurs, ainsi qu'il convient, renvoyez-moi la responsabilité de toute que vous aurez du faire: nous Elisa Segnini • Ethnicity, Gender, and a Decadent Canon oserons avec Mme Deledda ce que nous avons osé jamais avec Gabriele D'Annunzio, dont la prose, si je ne me trompe pas, avait un autre valeur intrinsèque et absolue que celle de notre petite Sarde. . . . Heureux ces Italiens, de vous avoir pour collaborateur autant et plus que pour traducteur" (Trim and cut as you wish and according to your artistic scruples. Mme Deledda, I am sure, will benefit from it. And, as agreed, blame me for what you will have to do. We will dare with Mme Deledda what we have never dared with Gabriele D'Annunzio, whose prose, if I am not mistaken, had a different intrinsic and absolute value than that of our little Sardinian. Happy these Italians, to have you as a collaborator as well a translator). 71 The sentence omitted by Hérelle in his memoirs is not only denigrating toward Deledda, but also reveals that his relationship to Brunetière went beyond reciprocal trust. As Loué and Wilfred-Portal have argued with reference to D'Annunzio, the two men censored and "domesticated" Italian writers under the pretext of avoiding offense to the sensibility of readers of the Revue des Deux Mondes. Moreover, the sentence demonstrates their belief in an "intrinsic and absolute" value of literature and shows that, as eminent French intellectuals, Hérelle and Brunietière saw themselves as gatekeepers of that value, even more so if this literature came from a culture implicitly considered inferior.

As Rasera notes, the highly figurative language Hérelle used in his correspondence with Brunetière betrays an almost sadistic enjoyment in this conglomerate role as editor and coauthor: he is inspired by a "courage destructeur" (destructive courage), describes his attitude as "cruel" and "sanguinaire" (bloodthirsty), and refers to the cuts to Cenere as "executions" or "hécatombe" (slaughter). 72 Despite the fact that Deledda was already living in Rome at the time in which she wrote the novel, Hérelle was outraged that she dared to set her novel anywhere other than Sardinia: "Pourquoi diable cette femme sarde, excellente quand elle parle de Sardegne, se mêle-telle de décrire la vie d'un étudiant romain, dont elle n'a guère l'idée?" (Why on earth does this Sardinian woman, excellent when she speaks of Sardinia, get involved in describing the life of a Roman student, of which she has no idea?). 73 Commenting on the chapters that describe the studies of the protagonist in Cagliari, he raves: "Si du moins le séjour était l'occasion d'une belle description de la ville sarde, on pourrait encore en excuser l'inutilité pour l'amour de l'art. Mais, après avoir lu ces pages, on n'a pas la moindre idée nette de Cagliari ; on a seulement lu deux ou trois promenades romantiques sur le collines avoisinantes et on a contemplé quelques couchers de soleil, une mer aux reflets métalliques, etc. Ce n'est pas plus

div.head: M O D E R N P H I L O L O G Y
div.p: Cagliari que n'importe quelle ville de la Méditerranée" (If at least the stay was the occasion for a beautiful description of the Sardinian city, one could still excuse its uselessness for the love of art. But, having read these pages, one does not have the slightest idea of Cagliari; we've only read a couple of romantic walks on the surrounding hills and watched some sunsets, a sea with metallic reflections, etc. It's no longer Cagliari, it is any city in the Mediterranean). 74 From this it can be seen that Hérelle's corrections aim to make Deledda's novel appear "plus vrai" (more real) and closer to the pictoresque descriptions of verismo. In other words, he sought to shift her work further away from decadent and symbolist influences. 75 Compare this with his treatment of D'Annunzio. For the translation of Trionfo della morte, Hérelle and Brunetière adopted the opposite strategy and cut the scene of pilgrimage to the Abruzzo sanctuary of Casalbordino, where D'Annunzio indulged in descripions of the animalistic behavior of the pilgrims. 76 The realism of the scene, in Brunetière's and Hérelle's view, was considered too brutal, too close to Zola's naturalism, and likely to offend the sensitivity of French readers. In D'Annunzio's case, the fact that such details were site specific was not, in their eyes, a redeeming quality. Deledda's response was to defend Cenere, describing her protagonist as "un'anima moderna, sovrapposta all'anima di un sardo indeciso ed egoista; l'anima moderna con tutte le sue malattie, con le sue indecisioni, le contraddizioni, gli istinti di bene e male, lo scetticismo, l'egoismo, la stanchezza, la debolezza, lo scontento, il vuoto che tutti i giovani moderni abbiamo nell'anima" (a modern soul, superimposed on the soul of an impulsive and selfish Sardinian; the modern soul with all its maladies, with its indecisions, contradictions, instincts of good and evil, skepticism, selfishness, weariness, weakness, discontent, the emptiness that all of us, modern young people, have in our soul). 77 This shows how Anania differs from the Sardinian protagonist of Elias Portolu and La via del male. While he happens to be Sardinian, the protagonist of Cenere represents the universal decadent hero, characterized by an impasse of the will, influenced by Nietzsche's Zarathustra. Cenere, Deledda insisted, was not a regional novel: "l'ho collocato in Sardegna perché è il paese che meglio conosco, ma poteva accadere anche a Roma o a Parigi" (I set it in Sardinia because it is the country I know best, but it could also take place in Rome or Paris). 78 But Deledda was ignorant of Hérelle's firm belief that "il ne faut jamais traduire un roman, fût-il d'ailleurs intéressant et bien fait, lorsque ce roman . . . pourrait aussi bien avoir été écrit à Paris qu'à Rome ou qu'à Madrid" (one should never translate a novel, no matter how interesting and well written, when this novel . . . could just as well have been written in Paris as in Rome or Madrid). 79 Hérelle saw D'Annunzio as a "genius" who could be treated as an exception, but these examples show how Deledda, instead, was not expected to engage with the urban, to assimilate modernist influences such as Dostoevsky (or indeed, D'Annunzio), or to set her novels beyond Sardinia.

In a letter from Gaston Calmann Lévy to Hérelle, we learn that the latter, by 1906, had decided he would no longer translate anything by Deledda. 80 But Deledda, probably guessing that Brunetière was more lenient toward her prose than Hérelle, had written directly to the director of La Revue des Deux Mondes about her last novel, L'ombra del passato (The shadow of the past) (1907), set in the Po Valley, and obtained from him an expression of interest. As the official translator of Deledda, Hérelle was obliged to translate the novel, but he did not appreciate it. Deledda defended it by asserting that it was not "un romanzo di ambiente e di costume" (a novel of mores and customs). As she had done with Cenere, she defined the protagonist as "un'anima moderna" (a modern soul) and noted that, as such, he differed from the "tipi primitivi" (primitive types) that still existed in Sardinia. The novel, she argued, followed a new poetics inspired by the change of setting. It did not set out to portray the violent passions of Sardinia, but the subdued emotions of the pianura padana: "Ne L'ombra del passato io ho voluto scrivere un romanzo diverso dagli altri, senza delitti, senza forti passioni, senza tipi nevrastenici né patologici, un romanzo che si svolge nello sfondo monotono ed uguale della pianura dalla quale devono prendere . . . l'intonazione e la linea" (With L'ombra del passato I aimed to write a novel that was different from the others, without crimes, without strong passions, without neurasthenic or pathological types, a novel that takes place in the monotonous and flat background of the plain from which they must take . . . their intonation and shape). 81 But Hérelle, as we have seen, had learned from D'Annunzio to appreciate "neurasthenic or pathological types," and was convinced that Deledda could only write competently about Sardinia.

Meanwhile, Brunetière had died, and Francis Charmes had taken up the editorship of the Revue des Deux Mondes. In his letters to Hérelle, Charmes agreed with the translator that the novel had too many lengthy passages, repetitions, and childish overtones. He encouraged Hérelle to take extensive measures, believing that Deledda's novel "gagnera certainement à passer en français sous une forme intermédiaire entre la traduction et l'adaptation" (will certainly benefit from being transposed into French in an intermediate form between translation and adaptation). 82 Such advice clearly reveals collusion among male colleagues to intervene in the work of an Italian woman writer to such an extent that it supersedes "translation" by a considerable degree. Hérelle's alterations confirm this. He cut references to current events and religion, descriptions of landscapes in which nature takes on a symbolist tone, sensual fantasies, scenes that dwell on characters' psychology, and passages echoing D'Annunzio.

He also omitted a passage in which the protagonist wonders whether he has become "degenerate," a detail that resonated with D'Annunzio's pathological characters. 83 The novel was serialized in the Revue des Deux Mondes during 1908 and published by Calmann-Lévy in 1909 with the revised title Le fantôme du passé (The ghost of the past). Like Serao, Deledda continued to offer her novels to Hérelle, and Hérelle continued to give her negative feedback. Deledda protested in vain that Sardinia was changing and, as a consequence, the protagonists of her novels were also changing, and that they were not necessarily "degenerate." Interestingly, she never offered to Hérelle Canne al vento (1913), a work to which she was particularly attached, and in which, more than any other, she experimented with symbolist aesthetics and musical prose. The examples discussed here, however, show that his appreciation was limited. As a male translator, working with other male colleagues in the field of publishing, editing, and translation, he felt able to intervene extensively in the work of these female writers. In translating their works, he did not hesitate to cut musical passages, descriptions of landscapes that resonated with symbolist aesthetics, and references to European writers; he expressed disapproval of Nietzsche's influence; and his linguistic strategies also contributed to tone down decadent and symbolist elements in Serao's and Deledda's work by standardizing their hybrid language, or by emphasizing dialect terms as ethnographic tokens.

Hérelle's role as translator produced a mixed legacy. He helped to disseminate work by Italian writers in French and, as such, he was instrumental 82. Deledda was already well known when Hérelle became interested in her writing (in 1926 she would become the first Italian woman to receive the Nobel Prize). Her focus on the ancient mores of Sardinia, the popular setting of her novels, and her engagement with dialect link Deledda to the school of verismo. She had, however, grown up reading French Romantic literature and D'Annunzio. Like her symbolist and decadent contemporaries, Deledda experimented with musical prose, creating landscapes infused with a sense of the magical and filling her novels with references to European literature. From Cenere (Ashes)(1900), onward, this included Nietzsche and Schopenhauer. Like D'Annunzio, she created characters marked by powerful sensuality and primitive passions, although in Deledda's work erotic transgression is mostly confined to the imagination, and her novels are characterized by a strong sense of morality. The aristocratic environment that characterized D'Annunzio's and Fogazzaro's novels was beyond the scope of the Sardinian writer. It is also, however, true that an ethnic element was not alien to Italian decadentismo, as testified by the

note.p: many references to Abruzzo in D'Annunzio's works, from entire episodes of Trionfo della morte to dramas such as La figlia di Iorio (Iorio's daughter) (1903), and La fiaccola sotto il moggio (The torch under the bushel) (1905). Deledda exemplifies this rural engagement with decadence, since many of her texts apply decadent themes and motifs to Sardinian contexts.

div.p: in the transnational and international spread of decadence and symbolism; he did so, however, emphatically upon his own terms and in ways that diminished the transgressive aspects of those works he translated. This is also true of his dealings with D'Annunzio, but the examples discussed here demonstrate the greater degree to which he felt able to make such editorial interventions when it came to working with women writers.

Furthermore, in contrast with his treatment of Deledda and Serao, Hérelle did not expect D'Annunzio to provide picturesque descriptions of rural environments. In D'Annuzio's case, Hérelle acknowledged that the aristocratic world of his novels did not have much local color. He and his collaborators accepted that the background of D'Annunzio's works could vary from Abruzzo to Tuscany to Rome to Venice. In contrast, despite the fact that numerous novels by Serao featured the Roman or international aristocracy, and that a third of Deledda's production was set outside of Sardinia, he had no tolerance for works by these writers that was not preoccupied with their native regions.

Despite an apparent openness to new configurations of gender and sexuality, Hérelle thus took a highly conservative approach to his professional relationship with Deledda and Serao, and used his authority as a French male critic to censor those features of their work most closely affiliated with decadence and avant-garde culture. His practice, backed by the editors of prestigious French journals, denied Deledda and Serao their cosmopolitan scope. Despite Serao's and Deledda's international reputation and deep knowledge of European culture, this eclectic intellectual did not envision for their novels an afterlife in translation beyond an ethnic frame. To achieve the international recognition that came with Hérelle's name as a translator, Serao and Deledda accepted interventionist editing that granted them access to prestigious journals such as La Revue de Paris and La Revue des Deux Mondes. This intercession, however, also effaced the tension between verismo and decadentismo that characterized their novels, and created a stronger barrier between their writing and that of D'Annunzio than actually existed.
